Fund distributions: follow the cash, the unit value and the total resources

Explore why a fund payout is different from investment performance, how cash distributions affect unit NAV, and what changes when payments are retained or reinvested.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a fund’s distributions, unit value and total resources

Interactive planning lab

The annual total-return input is converted to monthly growth before a fixed per-unit distribution. That payment is initial unit NAV × scheduled annual distribution % ÷ 12. One holder retains cash outside at zero interest; the other reinvests every payment at the post-distribution NAV. Neither consumes cash or adds money. The central idea

A distribution moves value out of the fund. Read the remaining investment together with the cash received, and distinguish the payment schedule from the return earned.

01

Keep three different measurements in view

A fund can send cash to its investors while its unit value declines. That combination raises a useful question: how much value remains in the investment, how much has moved outside it, and how have the two together changed? Looking at only the payout or only the unit price leaves part of the answer out.

A distribution is a payment from a fund to its holders. Net asset value, or NAV, describes the value remaining per unit. Total return measures investment performance with distributions included under the stated calculation convention. These measurements have different denominators and should not be substituted for one another.

The SEC’s fund-distributions bulletin explains the general mechanics: payments transfer value to holders, reinvestment buys additional shares, and a high distribution rate does not establish strong performance. This article uses those mechanics in an independent CAD illustration; it does not apply U.S. reporting or tax rules to Canadian accounts.

02

Define the cash schedule before comparing percentages

The illustration begins with CAD 100,000 invested at a hypothetical NAV of CAD 10, giving the holder 10,000 units. The selected scheduled annual distribution is 8% of the initial NAV. That produces CAD 0.80 per original unit annually, paid as twelve equal monthly amounts of about CAD 0.066667.

The holder of the original 10,000 units therefore receives about CAD 666.67 each month, CAD 8,000 each year and CAD 40,000 over five years. Calculations retain full precision and use fractional units; displayed dollars are rounded. Neither the monthly amount nor the annual schedule is a promise from an actual fund.

The schedule uses the initial CAD 10 NAV throughout. It is not 8% of each later month’s changing fund value. This distinction matters when reading a yield-like label: identify the payment numerator, the price or NAV denominator, and the period before comparing percentages. The calculator’s distribution percentage is a cash-setting input, separate from its performance assumption.

03

Reconcile the fund value with cash retained outside

The independent performance assumption is a constant 5% effective annual fund total return before investor costs. The model converts it to an equivalent monthly growth factor. Each month, the unit NAV first grows by that factor and then the scheduled per-unit distribution is deducted.

For a holder who keeps the original units and retains every payment in outside cash earning zero interest, the five-year fund value is about CAD 82,419.00. The outside cash totals CAD 40,000. Together, the holder has approximately CAD 122,419.00, before taxes and costs.

The waterfall reconciles the fund-only endpoint: CAD 100,000 initially invested, plus about CAD 22,419.00 of cumulative investment growth on the changing fund balance, less CAD 40,000 transferred outside. The distribution is already included in the outside asset. Adding it again as extra investment profit would count the same cash twice.

The unit NAV finishes around CAD 8.24. That price alone omits the cash transferred to the holder. Conversely, calling the entire CAD 40,000 of payments profit would omit the reduction in resources remaining in the original units.

04

Compare retaining cash with reinvesting each payment

The second holder starts with the same CAD 100,000 and receives the same per-unit distribution policy. Every payment is immediately reinvested at the post-distribution NAV, so the holder acquires additional fractional units instead of accumulating outside cash.

In this frictionless illustration, reinvestment preserves full exposure to the assumed fund return. The ending value is CAD 100,000 × 1.05 to the fifth power, or approximately CAD 127,628.16. The difference from the collect-and-retain outcome is about CAD 5,209.16.

That difference comes from the different subsequent investment exposure of the distributed money. It is not an additional return created by the payment itself. Both holders receive the same assumed fund growth factors, but the first moves part of the resources into zero-interest cash.

A fair comparison must state what happens to payments. Spending them, earning interest elsewhere, paying tax or incurring reinvestment charges would change the household outcome. None occurs in this example. Both charts retain all resources, and neither holder supplies new money after the opening investment.

05

Change the payout and return assumptions independently

The comparison chart varies the scheduled distribution from 0% to 10% of initial NAV while holding the selected return and horizon fixed. Under the default positive return, larger cash distributions move more resources away from later fund growth. The fully reinvested endpoint remains the same across those hypothetical schedules.

Set the annual total return to zero. With the default distribution and horizon, the original-unit fund value becomes CAD 60,000 and outside cash becomes CAD 40,000. Total resources remain CAD 100,000. The payment has rearranged the resources without producing investment growth.

With a negative return assumption, cash moved outside at zero interest can cushion losses relative to leaving everything exposed to that invented declining path. That result does not identify a preferred payout policy for an uncertain future. Real returns vary, distributions can change, and money needed for spending may require a different plan.

06

Use the charts to ask better questions about an actual fund

The model does not classify any payment as interest, dividends, capital gains or return of capital for tax purposes. A falling NAV, or a scheduled payout above an assumed return, cannot by itself establish the tax character of a real distribution. Fund records and applicable account and tax rules are needed for that separate question.

For an actual investment, inspect the distribution policy, whether amounts can change, the treatment of reinvestment and the performance calculation being presented. Check whether quoted returns already deduct fund expenses and which investor-level costs remain outside them.

Finally, connect the investment to the spending plan. Cash delivered on a schedule can help fund bills, but its convenience does not determine whether total resources are growing or shrinking. Track what remains invested, what has been received, what has been spent, and what is still available. These four charts keep that reconciliation visible before attaching a performance label to a payout.
